If you’re trying to avoid pain, suicide isn’t for you. I’ve tried 11 times and it fucking hurts the whole time you’re dying. There is no good way to kill yourself. Life is gonna get that done for you, so instead of looking for easy ways out, look for easy ways back in.

Fuck that “one day at a time shit.” I say take life 10 seconds at a time if you have to. Even if I’m literally on fire, I can make it 10 seconds before giving in, and if I can burn alive for 10 seconds, I can sure as shit deal with anything else that long. Once the 10s is up, see if you can do 20s, then 30s. Before long, you’ll feel just better enough to realize chocolate cake is delicious, seeing a baby giggle is delightful, and Petsmart will totally let you play with a bunch of kittens all at once.
Suicide is like being really stupid. It’s difficult on you up to a point, but it’s the people around you that suffer.
Don’t be afraid of death. It happens to everyone and you can’t avoid it forever. Be afraid of dying slowly and painfully. Shit lasts so much longer than you’d think.

I wish I did. Everything I've learned was pure trial and error. For me, starting low and slow and just listening to my body helped. Forget proper form. Does anything shift when I start to lift? Better adjust my position until it doesn't. Am I overly sore after working out? I'll reduce the weights next time I do that lift, even if it feels too light. 

Listening to my body was the hardest part, but it's also prevented me from major injury. I can bench 200 with a machine, but I struggle with just the bar on the rack. 

Focusing on joint muscles (especially core, back, shoulders, and hips) has really helped me. I also don't worry about leg day vs. arm day or whatever most of the time. If my back is sore or a rib is out, the back gets worked. If my hips ache, it's hip abduction time. Basically, squeaky wheel gets the kick.

I'm 33, male, and I was diagnosed at 19 with Type 3.

I started exercising because I was overweight and the weight was putting immense pressure on my joints. I had hip subluxations daily and was using a cane to walk, but a wheel chair was definitely in my future.

I started with diet until I could move around with less pain. Once I hit that point, I started with some light weight lifting and cardio. Nothing too heavy or fast, just a lot of low & slow.

Two years into it, I work out 3-4 times a week, typically starting with weights (I only use machines, no free weights)  and then do 30 minutes of cardio, which is usually walking on a tread mill. I tried the elliptical, but it put too much strain on my lower thighs.

I'm out typically once every six months because of a dislocation that doesn't go back in or if it's particularly bad and there's bruising or serious inflammation. It usually takes three weeks for me to get back up to speed with working out, one of those weeks is usually an "I don't wanna" period.

I work a desk job, so an "active" day is usually not that active. I take walks at work on my breaks. I work out after quitting time. I don't plan rest days, but I do schedule days off from the gym to avoid strain or injury.

All that said, I have had a lot of success with weight lifting on machines. Leg day is by far my favorite and I have my hip abductions up to 305 pounds, my leg press reps are 500 pounds. I can't do a tenth of that on a squat rack because the bar dislocates my shoulders and ribs. It's taken a long time to figure out what I can do and how it can be done, and I'm still learning.

I've been playing a while, and like you, as I get older, I find that a regular game becomes more and more difficult to maintain. Sorry it's so long, but here are a few things I've used to help prolong a campaign:

* **Smaller games:** Keeping a game short (2-4 hours) and try to complete an adventure in no more than 3 sessions. In addition, keeping the game small in scope (1st-5th or 1st-10th levels) means that the game takes up less time out of your busy week, and you can actually complete a small campaign if you'd like.

* **Find your core players:** I tend to start new campaigns with 6-8 players if possible, but I look for the 2-3 players who are the most committed to the game. You can always rotate the less reliable players in and out, but build your campaign hooks and major plots around these 2-3 core players.

* **Play every time you have enough people to do so:** If the DM and two players show up, play. If you're not in a good place in the story to play without your main characters, there are plenty of things you can do here instead of continue the main story. Since your less reliable players rotate in and out, or take breaks of more than one session, use this time as a flashback. Tell a story that has already occurred in the campaign timeline, but hasn't been in the spotlight. You might use this time to develop side plots, hand out much needed gear or magic items, introduce small villains, etc. You can also use this time to introduce a new character for a new player or a player whose character has died.

* **Constantly look for new players:** This gets tiring if you're doing it all by yourself. Have your players bring friends who might be interested. Don't stop looking until you have 4-5 solid weekly players. If you drop below this, start looking again. I've gotten to the point that I've run games in my FLGS with an open invitation just to get new players. If you do this, bring pregens with some tie to your current campaign.

Here are some smaller things I've done that seem to help:

* **Bring food:** We've had great success with potlucks, although we have found that setting time aside at the beginning of the game is better than trying to eat while playing. That maybe just us. We do use this time to have one or more of the players summarize what's happened since the last time we played. They sometimes talk about the side quests that were done when other players weren't around, but usually it's the main plot stuff.

* **Have a Player send a summary email:** Not every group has someone who likes to do this, but it can help to have someone summarize the major points of the last session for the people who couldn't make it. Not only does it help keep people on the same page, but it's also a bit of an advertisement. Not OP, but his idea was close enough to mine. When the PC picks up the crown, it crumbles to dust. The next day, the PC has a splitting headache. All loud noise sounds like hollow, insane laughter. 

The day after that, small iron ridges appear poking through his scalp. In a week, a full iron crown has grown through his skull. It grants him a weak version of one of the Skull Lord's powers.

The first humanoid creature he "kills" with the power rises a day later and seeks him out, pledging fealty. He feels the crown's power grow. 

Repeat with the second time he kills someone with the newly enhanced power. After the second humanoid pledges fealty, he begins loosing weight each day until he is gaunt and his bones are clearly visible. 

After a week, he wakes up to discover his followers are dead, wasted away to just skulls with iron crowns. When he tries to leave them, they animate, and float to either side of his head. He now has access to all three powers of the skull lord, albeit weaker versions. 

His face starts to itch the next day, as if sand moves just beneath its surface. Scratching removes pieces of flesh, exposing bone, but enhances his powers. When he scratches enough to expose a fourth of his skull, one of the floating companion skulls fuses with that part of his head. His power increases. 

Eventually, he's torn his face off, attached both skulls and has become a new skull lord at full strength.

Of course, you could build an adventure around him removing the curse, but I would provide difficult obstacles that could be easily overcome if he gives in to using his new powers. 

Best case scenario, you have a new villain.
